lines.content: This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* Level of programming experience: [to be filled]
* IDE and level of expertise: [to be filled]
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.
* Give every commit a meaningful subject. Aim for 50 characters or fewer; do not exceed 72 characters.
* Write the subject in the imperative mood, capitalize its first word, and do not end it with a period.
* Add a scope or category prefix when useful, such as `Inventory: Add equipment units` or `chore: Document branch naming rules`. Capitalize the first word after the prefix.
* For non-trivial commits, include a body after a blank line and wrap it at 72 characters.
* Use the body to explain what changed and why, not how. Give enough context for a reader to judge the change without reading the diff.
* Structure the body as: current situation (present tense), why it needs to change, the change (imperative), why this approach was chosen, and any other relevant context.

Follow [Conventional Branch 1.1.0](https://conventionalbranch.org/) for new branches. Use lowercase names in the form `<type>/<description>`, with hyphens between words and no spaces or underscores. Include a zero-padded issue number when the work has one, using `issue-NN` before the short description. For example: `feature/issue-08-add-equipment-unit`.

Keep descriptions concise and descriptive. Mainline branches such as `main`, `master`, and `develop` do not use a prefix. Prefer the full prefixes listed above over the site's short aliases (`feat/` and `fix/`) for consistency in this project.
LabLog is a command-line application for laboratory technicians who manage
loanable electronics equipment. It supports equipment and borrower registration,
equipment copying, editing and relocation; single-unit and batch lending/returns;
renewals, loss reports, overdue listings and loan audit queries; reservations,
waiting requests, fault reports and repairs; validated import/export; and command recall.
Enter `help` in either the main LabLog console or the standalone borrower console
for a concise list of current LabLog commands. Enter `help COMMAND`, such as
`help loan`, for its syntax, fields, and explained usage examples. `help return`
shows returns with and without reported faults; `help add-borrower` demonstrates
both the usual and reordered fields. Help displays these examples without
The list identifies which console supports each command. Equipment registration
uses either a complete `add ASSET_ID n/NAME c/CATEGORY m/MODEL l/LOCATION`
command or the prompted `add ASSET_ID` form.
* `add-borrower BORROWER_ID n/NAME p/PHONE e/EMAIL` registers a borrower, rejects duplicate IDs, and saves validated contact details.
* `edit-borrower BORROWER_ID [n/NAME] [p/PHONE] [e/EMAIL]` updates validated contacts without changing the borrower ID.
* `commands` and `recall INDEX` display recent session input for explicit resubmission.
* `loans BORROWER_ID` lists a registered borrower's active loans, ordered by due date and then asset ID. Returned loans are excluded, and a loan is overdue only after its due date.

Borrower IDs follow the form `A0123456X`: an uppercase letter, seven digits, and an uppercase letter. Names contain 1-100 characters, phone numbers contain exactly eight digits, and email addresses use `u.nus.edu`. All three prefixes are required, may appear in any order, and must occur only once.
The standalone borrower console remains available for borrower registration and
lookup, and starts with its own empty loan book. In the main console, borrower
records are shared with loan commands and persist in the complete LabLog snapshot.

neither participates in a search. The command shares the record books, rather

The accepted form is `search TEXT`, where `TEXT` is non-empty and may contain
spaces. The handler trims the command line, checks the command word boundary,
and treats the remainder as one phrase. It collapses runs of whitespace in
both the query and searchable fields, then converts them with
`Locale.ROOT` before comparing. A candidate matches when its normalized name
or model contains the normalized query. This gives case-insensitive substring
matching that does not depend on the user's machine locale. Thus `search Ba`
matches “Basys3”; `search b3` does not, because initials and acronym matching
are outside the current US15 behavior.
The handler scans equipment in the order returned by `Inventory` and does not
sort the matches. This matches the default `list` order and makes results
predictable without an extra ordering option. If the inventory is empty, the
handler returns `No equipment registered.`; if it is non-empty but nothing
matches, it returns a separate message containing the normalized query. A
successful result uses the same columns as `list`: asset ID, name, category,
The scan is linear in the number of equipment units, with each comparison
bounded by the lengths of the name, model, and query. A precomputed search
index could reduce lookup time for a very large inventory, but would introduce
another representation to update after registration, edits, imports, and
future replacement workflows. For this small command-line inventory, scanning
the authoritative snapshot is simpler and cannot become stale. Adding search
options to `list` was also considered. A separate command keeps free-form
phrases distinct from `list`'s structured exact-value filters and sort options.
Availability is evaluated only for matching units and follows the shared
priority rule: a lost unit is displayed as `Lost`; otherwise an active loan is
`On loan`; otherwise an unresolved severe fault is `Unavailable: severe fault`;
all remaining units are `Available`. Reservations do not affect this
undated display. Since the handler does not cache status, an earlier search
cannot leave stale values for a later one.
Malformed syntax and an empty phrase raise `IllegalArgumentException` with
usage guidance. `LabLog` catches that expected validation exception at the
command boundary, prints an error, and continues the console loop. The code
does not use Java assertions for input checks: assertions can be disabled at
runtime, so user mistakes must continue to be rejected through ordinary
validation. Nor does the handler catch unexpected runtime failures; allowing
programming errors to surface is preferable to presenting them as normal
no-match results. At present, invalid searches are reported to the console but
do not produce a search-specific `FINE` log entry.
